p.seg: First
"Three Poems of Cherishing Feelings"
Heaven and Earth are vast and misty,
The primal essence cycles through seasons.
The bright sun shines with brilliance,
Gentle breezes sway at ease.
Bright light fills the sky,
Sweet dew blankets the land.
Lush and towering are the pines,
Graceful and long the thorny trees.
Insects in the grass mournfully chirp,
Orioles flutter their wings.
Moved by the times, thoughts arise,
I stand on tiptoe, gazing afar.
In the glorious imperial court,
Yī Héng serves as minister.
My talent is not fit for civil arts,
Nor my ability for martial ways.
I'll go to those Yuán and Xiāng rivers,
Entrusting myself to a fisherman's life.
Leisurely!
Carefree!
There I shall dwell and abide.
Second
The moon is bright, stars are sparse,
The sky is high, the air is cold.
Cassia flags and emerald banners,
Jade pendants and tinkling bells.
I rinse my hat strings in sweet springs,
Clothe myself in orchid and iris.
Longing to follow the two maidens,
I go to those Xiāng and Yuán rivers.
Spirits are hidden, hearing subtle,
Who can behold their jade-like faces?
Blazing are the spring blossoms,
Green leaves hold crimson within.
The sun and moon pass away,
Alas, your flourishing beauty!
Third
The clear wind sighs and moans,
The long night stretches endlessly.
I sing aloud, grieving at heart,
Alone I sleep, awake and speak.
Facing the cup, I beat my breast,
Before food, I forget to eat.
The world lacks day-lilies of comfort,
Making me sigh in sorrow.
Birds call, seeking companions,
"The Valley Wind" reproaches faults.
When Chóng Huá ascended to power,
The emperor ordered Kǎi Yuán.
Bào Shū opened his carriage shade,
Minister Guǎn aided Huán.
Huí and Bīn lamented Yú's plight,
Dare I not aspire to Yán's virtue!
My will holds to bright principles,
Not coveting official hats.
What is in my heart?
Its fragrance is like orchids.
First
"Eighty-two Poems of Cherishing Feelings"
In the night, I cannot sleep,
I rise and sit, playing my lute.
Thin curtains let the bright moon shine through,
The clear breeze blows through my lapel.
A lone swan cries in the wilds,
Soaring birds call in the northern woods.
Pacing, what shall I see?
Worried thoughts, alone and heartbroken.
Second
Two consorts stroll by the riverbank,
Carefree, they follow the wind, soaring.
Jiāo Fǔ untied their jade pendants,
Graceful and lovely, full of fragrance.
Enraptured by tender affection,
For a thousand years, not forgotten.
Their beauty captivated Xiàcài,
Lovely faces tied to heartfelt bonds.
Deeply moved, worries arise,
Day-lilies planted in orchid chambers.
For whom are the ointments applied?
Longing for rain, resentful of morning sun.
How can a bond strong as metal and stone,
Suddenly bring such parting sorrow?
Third
Under fine trees, paths naturally form,
In the eastern garden, peaches and plums.
Autumn winds blow the withering leaves,
From here begins their falling.
Even splendor must fade and wither,
Halls give way to thorns and brambles.
I whip my horse to leave this place,
Going up to the foot of Western Hills;
If I cannot protect myself,
How can I cling to wife and child!
Frost covers the wild grass,
As the year ends, all is said and done.
Fourth
A heavenly steed comes from the northwest,
Yet it follows the eastern road.
Spring and autumn have no fixed abode,
How can wealth and honor last forever?
Fresh dew bedews the marsh orchids,
Hard frost clings to the wild grass.
In morning, a charming youth,
By evening, ugly and old.
Unless one is Wáng Zǐ Jìn,
Who can remain forever fair?
Fifth
In my youth, in younger days,
Frivolous, I loved strings and songs.
Traveling west to Xiányáng,
With Zhào and Lǐ I passed my time.
Pleasures not yet at their end,
The bright day suddenly wasted away.
Driving my horse, I return again,
Looking back toward Sānhé.
Hundreds of yì in gold all spent,
Resources always too abundant.
Facing north on Tàiháng path,
Having lost my way, what shall I do!
Sixth
I've heard of the melons of Dōnglíng,
Near outside the Green Gate.
Rows upon rows between paths,
Mother and child linked together.
Five colors shine in the morning sun,
Honored guests gather from all sides.
Fat and fire bring their own torment,
Wealth and riches become calamities.
A commoner's life can last a lifetime,
Favor and emolument—can they be relied upon?
Seventh
In the sweltering heat of this summer,
Thirty days about to pass.
Fragrant trees hang with green leaves,
Blue clouds drift in winding trails.
The four seasons alternate in succession,
Sun and moon rise and set in turn.
Pacing in the empty hall,
Distressed, none knows my heart.
I wish to see joy and harmony endure,
Not witness the sorrow of parting.
Eighth
Blazing, the sun sets in the west,
Its remaining light clothes me.
Whirlwinds blow against four walls,
Cold birds cling to one another.
Zhōu zhōu birds still carry twigs in beaks,
Qíong qíong beasts also think of hunger.
How can those in high positions,
Bent like chime stones, forget their return!
Is it for boastful fame,
That haggardness brings heartache?
Rather soar with swallows and sparrows,
Than follow the yellow swan in flight.
The yellow swan roams the four seas,
Midway, where will it return?
Ninth
I walk out of the Shàngdōng Gate,
Gaze north toward Shǒuyáng's peak.
Below are hermits picking ferns,
Above, a fine grove of trees.
Where is the auspicious time?
Hard frost soaks my lapel.
Cold winds shake the mountain ridge,
Dark clouds gather, casting heavy shadows.
Honking geese fly southward,
Cuckoos utter mournful cries.
Plain essence wanders in autumn's voice,
Desolate, it wounds my heart.
Tenth
In Běilǐ, many exotic dances,
From Pú River, subtle music comes.
Frivolous, idle wanderers,
Now rising, now sinking in fortune.
Shortcuts through narrow paths,
They strive toward debauchery.
Where can one see Wáng Zǐ Qiáo,
Riding clouds over Dèng Forest?
Only the art of longevity,
Can comfort my heart.
Eleventh
Vast and deep flows the Long River's water,
Above which stands a grove of maple trees.
Orchids cloak the winding paths along the shore,
As a black steed gallops off with swift ease.
Gazing into the distance brings me sorrow,
The breath of spring stirs feelings in my heart.
In Sānchǔ, many talents did flourish,
Yet courtly clouds led to decadent art.
Crimson blooms exude their fragrant allure,
At Gāocài, pursuits of pleasure unfold.
I mourn for the oriole, unaware of peril,
Who can hold back these tears, a story told?
Twelve
In days of old, the lavish and the proud,
Ānlíng and Lóngyáng, in favor high.
Like peach and plum blossoms, tender and bright,
Radiant and splendid, they catch the eye.
Their joy like the nine springs of the year,
Bowing deep as autumn frost descends.
A glance that flows with grace and charm,
Words and laughter, like fragrance, they send.
Hand in hand, sharing love and delight,
Once sharing quilts through day and night.
Wishing to be a pair of birds in flight,
Soaring together, side by side in light.
In paintings, vows are clearly sworn,
Never to forget, from dusk to morn.
Thirteen
Ascending high, I overlook the wilds,
Gazing north toward the green hills' embrace.
Pine and cypress shade the ridge and mound,
Birds fly past, calling as they race.
My heart feels sorrow, bitter and deep,
Resentment and pain often hold me tight.
Lǐ Gōng mourned at the eastern gate,
Sū Zǐ confined in Sānhé's plight.
Seeking virtue, they found what they sought,
Why then sigh or lament their lot?
Fourteen
Autumn begins with a chill in the air,
Crickets chirp by the bed, a lonely sound.
Moved by nature, I harbor deep worries,
Quietly, sorrow in my heart is found.
To whom can I speak these many words?
Whom can I tell with phrases so profound?
A gentle breeze stirs my silken sleeves,
The bright moon shines with a clear, soft light.
At dawn, a cock crows from a tall tree,
I order my carriage to return in flight.
Fifteen
In past years, at fourteen or fifteen,
My ambition leaned to books and verse.
Clad in rough cloth, yet holding gems within,
With Yán and Mǐn, my hopes I'd immerse.
Opening my window to the wilds outside,
Climbing high to gaze where my thoughts reside.
Graves and mounds cover the hills and slopes,
All generations share the same end in stride.
After a thousand years, ten thousand more,
Where then does glory and fame abide?
Then I understand Xiànménzǐ's way,
And laugh at myself, in disarray.
Sixteen
Wandering by the Péng Pond's shore,
I turn to look toward Dàliáng afar.
Green waters surge with towering waves,
The wilderness stretches vague and char.
Beasts run wild, crossing every path,
Birds in flight follow, a scattered march.
At this time, the Quail Fire shines,
Sun and moon face each other, a celestial arch.
The north wind blows with bitter cold,
A frosty chill descends, dark and harsh.
A traveler with no companion near,
In every glance, I hold sorrow dear.
Petty men calculate their gains,
Noble ones uphold the constant chains.
Why fear ending worn and frail,
Chanting these lines, my truth I unveil.
Seventeen
Sitting alone in an empty hall,
Who can share joy with me at all?
Stepping out, I face the endless road,
No carriage or horse in sight bestowed.
Climbing high, I view the nine domains,
Vast and divided, the wild remains.
A lone bird flies toward the northwest,
Stray beasts southeast, in unrest.
At dusk, I think of friends and kin,
Hoping for words my heart to win.
Eighteen
The hanging chariot in the southwest glows,
Xīhé about to sink, the day will close.
Flowing light illuminates the seas,
Swiftly it reaches evening's ease.
At dawn, it bathed in Xiánchí's light,
Měngsǐ received its glory bright.
Who knows that scholars, poor or great,
Once dead, cannot regenerate?
Look at those peach and plum blooms fair,
Who can keep their brilliance rare?
Where is the noble man, I plea?
Sighing, we're not in harmony.
Gazing up at Jǐngshān's pines,
They can console these heartaches of mine.
Nineteen
In the west, there is a beauty rare,
Bright as the sunlight, pure and fair.
Clad in fine silken robes she wears,
With double huáng pendants, she compares.
Her adorned grace shines with delight,
A subtle fragrance wafts in the wind's light.
Ascending high, she gazes where thoughts lie,
Raising her sleeves to the morning sky.
Her image sent among the clouds on high,
Waving sleeves, she soars in the void to fly.
Drifting in a trance, elusive and deep,
Casting glances my way as I keep.
Joyful yet not in union true,
In silent words, my sadness grew.
Twenty
Yáng Zhū wept at the fork in the road,
Mò Zǐ grieved for the silk's dyed code.
Courtesies lead to long farewells,
Drifting apart, no one can tell.
Not just for tender love's sweet art,
Life and death play a vital part.
Desolation brings common grief,
Disasters come beyond belief.
Zhào's maiden charmed in Zhōngshān's land,
Humble and soft, more deceived she'd stand.
Alas, the scholar on the way,
How to safeguard himself, I say?
Twenty-One
In my heart, I cherish every moment's flight,
As Xīyáng approaches the end of light.
Waving my sleeve, I grasp my long sword,
Looking up to watch the floating clouds toward.
Among the clouds, a dark crane cries,
Lifting its will with mournful sighs.
Soaring once to pierce the azure sky,
Through ages, its voice will not reply.
How could it join quails and sparrows in play,
Fluttering in the courtyard day by day?
Twenty-Two
Xiàhòu rode in a cloud-borne carriage high,
Kuāfù became the Dèng Forest nigh.
Life and death follow changes' flow,
Sun and moon have their rise and low.
The phoenix sings in varied tone,
Línglún drew music, all his own.
Prince Wáng loved the panpipes' sound,
Generations seek what he had found.
Who says it cannot be seen?
The bluebird makes my feelings keen.
Twenty-Three
In the southeast lies Shè Mountain grand,
Fén River flows from its southern land.
Six dragons pull the breath-drawn car,
Cloud canopies touch heaven's bar.
Four or five immortals, free and bright,
At ease in orchid rooms, a peaceful sight.
Resting in pure harmony deep,
Breath in and out forms frost and dew heap.
Bathing in the Cinnabar Abyss,
They shine with sunlight and moonlight's kiss.
How can one rest at the Spirit Tower's height?
Roaming far, they soar in endless flight.
Twenty-Four
Deep worries knot my will and soul,
Fear and dread often take their toll.
Carefree moments not yet done,
The red sun suddenly west has run.
Crickets chirp by the window still,
Cicadas sing in the courtyard, shrill.
Hearts not in tune, no mutual grace,
Who can say they understand my case?
I wish to be a bird in clouds above,
Crying sorrowfully for miles with love.
Three fungi extend on Yíngzhōu's shore,
Roaming far may let me live evermore.
Twenty-Five
Drawing my sword to face the gleaming blade,
How could it possibly wound me?
I only fear the eloquent speakers,
Who slander me by the Sānjiāng's side.
Flying springs flow down the Jade Mountain,
The hanging chariot rests at Fúsāng.
Sun and moon traverse a thousand miles,
Pure winds bring a hint of frost.
Fortunes have their ups and downs,
Sighs and laments—how can they last?
Twenty-six
At dawn I climb the great slope's peak,
At dusk I gaze upon the western hills.
Thorns cover the plains and fields,
Flocks of birds flutter and fly.
Phoenixes and other birds roost in time,
Life follows its natural course.
Who can approach the Jiànmù tree?
The Shègān plant sways gracefully.
Do you not see the vines in the woods,
Spreading and intertwining?
Twenty-seven
Zhōu and Zhèng intersected under heaven,
Their streets aligned with the Sānhé region.
A charming and elegant youth,
How resplendent and fragrant!
Dark hair and a ruddy complexion,
A glance shines with brilliance.
The whole city longs for a look,
Gazing upon him with admiration.
I wish to roam through the spring,
But the morning sun suddenly fades.
Glory and decay in a moment,
How will we bear the parting?
Twenty-eight
Like flowers shining across the four seas,
Fúsāng shades Yíngzhōu.
Sun and moon traverse the celestial path,
Light and dark do not oppose each other.
Strictness and openness have their constants,
What more can one seek from gain or loss?
Why emulate the children on the road,
Holding hands and wandering together?
Yīn and yáng undergo changes,
Who says what sinks will not float?
The crimson turtle leaps in the flying spring,
Flying by night over Wúzhōu.
Bowing and rising, moving with heaven and earth,
Again I stroke the four seas' flow.
Bound by the arena of fame and gain,
Steeds and nags share the same shaft.
Better to cast aside sight and sound,
Ascend afar and leave behind deep sorrows.
Twenty-nine
Once I traveled to Dàliáng,
Ascended to the peak of Huánghuá.
Gònggōng dwelled in the dark depths,
A high tower reached the blue sky.
The desolate wilderness stretches endlessly,
Filled with grief for those I cherish.
Whom do I cherish?
One who sees clearly and reflects her own beauty.
The Yìnglóng sank in Jìzhōu,
The enchantress could not sleep.
Indulging in excess, defying the world,
How could one say her years would last forever!
Thirty
I drive my carriage out the gate,
Intending to journey far.
Where does this journey lead?
Turning my back on boastfulness and fame.
Boastful fame does not reside in me,
I only wish to follow my true feelings.
A single curtain blocks the bright sun,
A high tower muffles faint sounds.
Slander and deceit cause estrangement,
Floating clouds darken the day.
Graceful and charming, sharing the same robe,
A single glance could topple a city.
Ease and comfort last but a moment,
Splendor does not bloom twice.
Morning swiftly turns to dusk,
I no longer see my beloved's form.
The yellow bird flies southeast,
Sending a message to thank my friends.
Thirty-one
Setting off from the capital of Wèi,
Gazing south toward Chuītái.
The sound of flutes and pipes lingers,
But where is the King of Liáng now!
Soldiers eat chaff and husks,
The worthy dwell among the weeds.
Before the song and dance conclude,
The Qín troops return once more.
Jiālín is no longer ours,
Vermilion palaces gather dust.
Defeated beneath Huáyáng,
In the end, turned to dust and ashes!
Thirty-two
The morning sun does not shine twice,
The bright day suddenly darkens in the west.
Leaving this is like a nod,
How can it feel like nine autumns?
Human life is like dust and dew,
The way of heaven is vast and endless.
Qí Jǐng ascended the hill,
Tears and snivel streaming down.
Confucius faced the long river,
Lamenting the passage like a float.
Those who have gone, I cannot catch,
Those yet to come, I will not retain.
I wish to climb Tàihuà Mountain,
And roam with Sōngzǐ above.
The fisherman knew the world's troubles,
Drifting along in a light boat.
Thirty-three
One day follows another,
One evening follows another dawn.
My complexion changes from normal,
My spirit fades away.
In my chest, I harbor boiling fire,
Changes thus beckon.
All things are without end,
Wisdom and strategy are painfully scarce.
I only fear in a fleeting moment,
My soul will drift away with the wind.
Treading on thin ice all my life,
Who knows the anguish in my heart!
Thirty-four
One day follows another,
One dusk follows another dawn.
My appearance changes from normal,
My spirit drifts away.
Facing the cup, much sorrow and pain,
Missing my friends of old.
Before wine, I cannot speak,
Grieving, filled with bitterness.
I wish to till the fields east of the marsh,
But who will guard my truth with me?
Sorrow and suffering last but a while,
Noble conduct wounds the humble self.
What is the use of right and wrong?
Dragons and snakes are my neighbors.
Thirty-five
How chaotic are worldly affairs,
The human path is fraught with haste.
Prime years pass with time,
Like morning dew awaiting the sun.
I wish to grasp Xīhé's reins,
So the white sun does not shift its light.
The celestial steps are utterly remote,
The Milky Way vast with no bridge.
Washing my hair by Yánggǔ's shore,
Roaming afar by Kūnlún's side.
Climbing those immortal peaks,
Plucking these autumn orchids' fragrance.
Why strive for the worldly path?
In the Tàijí, one can soar freely.
Thirty-six
Who says all things are arduous?
Carefreeness can last a lifetime.
By the hall, shaded by blooming trees,
Serenely pondering the formless.
Wandering in thought of kin and friends,
Suddenly, darkness falls again.
Sending a word with the eastward flying birds,
May it comfort my feelings.
Thirty-seven
A fine time is this very moment,
Drizzling rain sprinkles the dust.
Gazing down the road for my beloved,
From dawn till dusk, still not coming.
Human emotions stir with feeling,
How can such turmoil be dispelled?
Wiping tears, nursing sorrow and grief,
Who can I tell of this bitterness!
Thirty-eight
Flaming light stretches ten thousand miles,
Mighty rivers surge through rapids wild.
A curved bow hangs upon the Fúsāng tree,
A long sword leans beyond the celestial sphere.
Tài Shān becomes a whetstone for the blade,
The Yellow River serves as a sash and belt.
Behold that Master Zhuāng Zhōu,
How can glory or decay be relied upon?
He cast his body away in the wilderness,
Where crows and kites brought harm and fear.
How can he compare to the heroic scholar,
Whose merit and fame from this grow vast?
Thirty-Nine
How fervent is the stalwart man,
His will aspires to awe the eight wild realms.
Driving his chariot on a distant campaign,
He forgets himself upon receiving the command.
A fine bow carries the Wūháo brand,
Bright armor gleams with radiant light.
Facing peril, he cares not for his life,
His body perishes, his soul soars high.
How could he be one who preserves his frame?
He gives his life contending on the battlefield.
Loyalty brings honor for a hundred generations,
Righteousness makes his fair name renowned.
Leaving his legacy to inform posterity,
His moral integrity thus endures eternal.
Forty
The Primordial Chaos gave birth to the Two Forms,
The Four Symbols revolve by the celestial pivot.
The bright sun spreads its fiery essence,
The pale moon casts its luminous glow.
The sundial's shadow moves in cycles clear,
Alas, how fragile is human life!
Drifting like dust swept by the wind,
Sudden as auspicious clouds that fade.
Long life would suit my wish indeed,
But glory and favor are not my own might.
Ānqī treads the heavenly path,
Sōngzǐ stands apart from the world.
How can I gain wings to reach the skies,
And flutter up to the clouded shores?
Alas, the aspiration of Confucius!
Why did he dwell among the Nine Barbarians?
Forty-One
Heaven's net spreads over the four wilds,
Six wings are folded, unable to stretch.
Drifting guests follow the waves in disarray,
Floating like ducks upon the water's face.
Life has no fixed span to count upon,
Morning and evening hold unforeseen perils.
Immortals halt the march of aging,
Nourishing their will in emptiness and void.
Soaring between the clouds and sun,
Far removed from the worldly path.
Glory and fame are not my treasures,
How can music and beauty bring me joy?
Gathering herbs, none return again,
The ambition for immortality proves false.
Faced with this, truly I am perplexed,
Leaving me long in hesitation deep.
Forty-Two
A king's enterprise needs able aides,
To achieve merit awaits heroic men.
Yuán and Kǎi brought peace and beauty,
Many scholars sang their praises loud.
Yin and Yang sometimes go astray,
Sun and moon do not always shine.
Heavenly times have rise and fall,
Human affairs know fullness and decline.
Yuán and Qǐ fled to the Southern Peak,
Bó Yáng hid in the Western Rong.
Preserving oneself reflects the true Way,
How can favor and splendor be esteemed?
Who does not start with good intent,
But few can bring it to an end.
Admirable are the scholars of ancient times,
For ten thousand years their pure fame lasts!
Forty-Three
Swans follow one another in flight,
Flying, flying to the distant frontiers.
Their wings meet the enduring wind,
In a moment, they vanish ten thousand miles.
At dawn, they feast on Lánggān fruit,
At dusk, they rest by Dān Shān's edge.
Lifting themselves amid the azure clouds,
What snare or net can hold them back?
How could they join the village scholars,
Hand in hand to make vows together?
Forty-Four
All things differ from start to end,
Long and short each have their own place.
Lánggān grows on the high mountains,
Zhīyīng blossoms brighten vermilion halls.
Glistening, the peach and plum flowers,
Form paths but soon will wither and fall.
How dare I hope for a thousand arts,
In three springs, a faint light I display.
Unless I am a tree that withstands the wind,
How can there be constancy in my decline?
Forty-Five
The secluded orchid cannot be worn,
For whom does the vermilion grass bloom?
Tall bamboos hide in the mountain's shade,
Shègān looks upon the layered walls.
Gé lěi vines spread through hidden valleys,
Melons and gourds grow in endless succession.
Joy at its peak consumes the spirit,
Deep sorrow wounds the human heart.
Knowing well that worry brings no gain,
Why not return to the Great Purity?
Forty-Six
The turtledove flies among mulberry and elm,
The seabird roams between heaven and earth.
Does it not know the vast and grand?
But its wings are not suited for such flight.
How can it soar with Zhāoyáo's grace?
Better to perch upon a tree's branches.
Below, it gathers among weeds and artemisia,
Above, it wanders garden fences and plots.
Yet even this brings its own contentment,
Why should it follow in your wake?
Forty-Seven
Where is the destiny of life to be found?
In sorrow and grief, tears soak my lapel.
High birds soar over mountain ridges,
Swallows and sparrows nest in the lower woods.
Azure clouds veil the front courtyard,
A plain qin grieves my heart with its tune.
On lofty hills, a crane calls clear,
But how can I hope to follow its path?
Forty-Eight
A dove plays among the courtyard trees,
The Jiāomíng wanders through floating clouds.
Where can one see a lone bird in flight,
Fluttering without a mate or flock?
Life and death follow nature's course,
How scattered and diverse their dispersal!
Forty-Nine
Strolling along the triple crossroads,
Melancholy, I ponder my beloved one.
Is it for a meeting today I long?
Vaguely, it feels truly possible.
In the marsh grows a tall pine tree,
For ten thousand years, it cannot be awaited.
High birds skim the heavens in flight,
Together they roam and play in the clouds.
How can there be a solitary wanderer,
Weeping in sorrow for times long past?
Fifty
Clear dew turns to凝固 frost,
Blossoming grass becomes withered weeds.
Who says the noble man is virtuous,
How can enlightenment and wisdom prevail?
Riding clouds, I summon Sōng and Qiáo,
Breathing in, may it last forevermore!
Fifty-One
A loyal heart loses its due reward,
Heavy virtue falls where it should not.
How can kind words long endure,
Benevolence and grace are hard to bestow.
Do you not see the south-flying swallows,
Their wings uneven in their flight?
Gāo Zǐ lamented in new verses,
Sān Lǘ mourned the parting ways.
Why did the Primordial Chaos Being,
Suddenly see its form and features destroyed?
Fifty-Two
Ten suns rise from the Yáng Valley,
Halting their pace, they race ten thousand miles.
Crossing the sky, they shine on the four seas,
Suddenly, they sink into the Měngsì's depths.
Who says the blazing heat lasts long,
Their journey's end awaits what course?
The departed, can they live forever?
They too leave behind thorns and brambles.
A thousand years are but a morning's span,
A single meal briefly sustains the self.
Between right and wrong, gain and loss,
How can they suffice for mutual scorn?
Calculating gain, I know my arts are exhausted,
Can sorrowful feelings ever cease?
Fifty-Three
Nature has its constant laws,
Life and death follow an unpredictable way.
Countless schemes and wits emerge,
Yet the essence remains unchanged.
How can those flattering sycophants,
Wear proud expressions with arrogant hearts?
Riding carriages drawn by fine horses,
Leaning on desks toward rich feasts.
Clad in delicate silk robes,
In deep pavilions and secluded rooms.
They do not see the evening blossoms,
Fluttering by the roadside.
Number Fifty-Four
Boasting talk eases resentment,
Laziness stirs a troubled heart.
Northwest, I ascend Bùzhōu Mountain,
Southeast, I gaze toward Dènglín.
Vast wilderness spans the nine regions,
Lofty mountains rival high peaks.
One meal spans ten thousand ages,
A thousand years rise and sink again.
Who says jade and stone are the same?
Tears fall, impossible to restrain.
Number Fifty-Five
People say they wish for long life,
But what is the purpose of extending years?
The yellow crane calls to Zǐ'ān,
A thousand autumns cannot be assured.
Sitting alone in the mountain cliffs,
Sorrowful, I cherish my thoughts.
How fine was the prince!
Gracefully, we supported each other.
Joyful as if it were this very day,
Yet plans were made for but a moment.
Setting aside tomorrow's affairs,
By evening, I am deceived.
Number Fifty-Six
Nobility and baseness lie in heaven's decree,
Poverty and success each have their time.
The charming, flattering, wicked ones,
Follow profit to deceive.
Lonely thoughts diminish kind deeds,
Only to be mocked by slanderers.
The wagtail cries in the clouds,
Flying with no destination in sight.
How can one know the fickle man,
May in a moment be unreliable?
Number Fifty-Seven
A startling wind shakes the four wilds,
Returning clouds shade the hall's corner.
For whom are the bed curtains set?
For whom are the cane and staff supported?
Though not a wise gentleman,
How could I be ignorant of the mulberry and elm?
The world has such deaf and blind,
Vast and boundless, where will they go?
Fluttering, they fly with the wind,
Drifting far from their old abode.
Departing beneath the Jade Mountain,
Abandoning slander and praise.
Number Fifty-Eight
A tall hat cuts through floating clouds,
A long sword reaches beyond the heavens.
Trivial matters not worth considering,
Soaring high across an era.
If not for you as my charioteer,
I'd wander freely in distant lands.
Bidding farewell to the Queen Mother of the West,
I shall depart from here onward.
How could I with the thatched hut scholar,
Strum the zither and recite vows?
Number Fifty-Nine
There is an old man by the river,
Who discarded pearls to weave reeds.
Content with coarse food,
Happy in his humble hut.
How could he emulate the frivolous ones,
Galloping fine horses in light carriages?
Born by the road in the morning,
Buried at the crossroad by evening.
Joy and laughter do not last the day,
In a moment, sighs return.
Reflecting on these two or three,
My indignation finds relief.
Number Sixty
Confucian scholars master the six arts,
Their resolve cannot be swayed.
They do not act against ritual,
Nor speak what is unlawful.
Thirsty, they drink from clear springs,
Hungry, they eat from a single basket.
With no means for seasonal sacrifices,
Their clothes often suffer cold.
In sandals, they sing the "South Wind,"
In worn robes, they laugh at ornate carriages.
Devoted to the Way, they uphold the classics,
Righteously refusing even a meal.
Fierce are the words of praise and blame,
Making the Daoist sigh deeply!
Number Sixty-One
In youth, I learned swordsmanship,
My skill surpassed Qūchéng's.
Heroic aura pierced the clouds,
Transcending the world with rare fame.
Wielding my sword in the desert,
Watering my horse in the wilds' borders.
How the banners flutter,
Only the sound of gongs and drums is heard.
The army's march brings sorrow,
Fierce and full of grief.
Thinking of my ordinary times,
Regret is born from this.
Number Sixty-Two
At noon, I adjust my attire,
Hoping to receive guests.
Who are these guests?
Vanishing like flying dust.
Robes adorned with cloud-like aura,
Words that delve into spirits and gods.
In an instant, they turn their backs,
When will I see such people again!
Number Sixty-Three
Too much worry scatters the will,
Solitude brings sorrow to the heart.
Soaring, I gaze over marshes,
Grasping my sword, I board a light boat.
I only wish for lasting leisure,
To return in later years and wander again.
Number Sixty-Four
At dawn, I leave the Shàngdōng Gate,
Gazing afar at the base of Shǒuyáng.
Pines and cypresses loom dense and deep,
Orioles play together.
Wandering freely through the nine bends,
Pacing, where shall I go?
Thinking of my usual days,
Melancholy, I long for the enchanting beauty.
Number Sixty-Five
The prince at fifteen years,
Roamed the shores of Yī and Luò,
Rosy cheeks bloomed like spring,
Witty and wise, embracing purity.
How could he see Fúqiū Gōng,
Raising his hand to bid farewell to the world?
Frivolous and easily bewildered,
Drifting, he abandoned his own self.
Flying, crying, and soaring,
Flapping wings with bitter sorrow.
Number Sixty-Six
The frontier gate cannot be passed,
How can the sea be crossed?
The bright summer does not appear,
Dark and obscure, alone without hope.
Holding a melon, I think of Dōnglíng,
The yellow sparrow truly feels ashamed.
Fortune lost in an instant,
I gird my sword and ascend Wúqiū.
Mourning for that Sānglínzǐ,
Tears flow in streams.
Borrowing a carriage between Qiān and Wèi,
With saddle and horse, I depart to wander.
Number Sixty-Seven
The grand scholar relies on systems,
Clothed in proper, constant attire.
Noble and base set in order,
All things aligned with principles.
Adornments tidy, complexion neat,
Bowing low, holding jade tablets.
In the hall, plain wine is placed,
In the room, fine grains abound.
Outwardly, he preaches integrity,
Indoors, the fragrance fades.
Words slip out from the heart,
Then again, he speaks of morality.
The twisted, circling etiquette,
Its postures trouble my soul.
Number Sixty-Eight
Northward I face the Dry Gleam Creek,
Westward I roam to Lesser Ren.
Gazing afar toward the Heavenly Ford,
My heart delights in its carefree waves.
Luxuriant lies the gate of life and death,
A single passage, never to be retraced.
Should I meet the morning wind bird,
I'd fly my carriage from southern woods.
In the vast shimmer of Jade Light,
Swiftly I'd indulge in wild abandon.
Resting serene in the Pure Capital,
Who could forbid transcending the world?
Number Sixty-Nine
People know how to form bonds,
But true friendship is uniquely hard.
Dangerous paths are full of doubts,
Bright pearls cannot be easily sought.
They crave a grand feast's offerings,
While I desire but a simple meal.
Loss and gain breed bitter resentment,
What more is there to say in dismay?
Number Seventy
Where there is sorrow, there is feeling,
Without sorrow, thought too ceases.
Unless entangled in nets and snares,
Why venture to distant borders?
Soaring winds brush the highest heavens,
Auspicious clouds beckon the dawn.
With a withered heart lodged in a dry abode,
Why care for mortal appearances?
To begin forgetting oneself is hard,
How can one know silent self-release?
Number Seventy-One
Hibiscus blooms gloriously on the mound,
Radiant with brilliant hues.
The white sun sinks in the woods,
Petals flutter down by the roadside.
Crickets chirp by the window,
Cicadas sing among thorns.
Mayflies sport for but three dawns,
Glistening, they groom their wings.
For whom do they adorn their robes?
Bowing and rising, they tidy themselves.
How long does life truly last?
With fervor, each strives their best.
Number Seventy-Two
On long roads, fine carriages speed,
Great rivers bear light boats.
Is life and death by nature's course?
Circumstances dictate the path.
High renown confounds the will,
Heavy profits burden the heart.
Even kin harbor doubts,
Flesh and blood turn to foes.
Better to shatter pearls and jade,
And use them to roam freely.
Number Seventy-Three
On the broad way, an extraordinary scholar,
A yellow steed draws his carriage.
At dawn, he rises in Yíngzhōu's wilds,
By dusk, he rests in Brilliant Light.
Again he traverses the four seas,
His wings soaring on their own.
Setting aside worldly affairs,
How could they trouble my heart?
Once gone, long severed,
For a thousand years, we'll gaze again.
Number Seventy-Four
Oh, the scholars of ancient times,
Serene and content in poverty.
In latter days, the Way declined,
Rushing amid dust and grime.
Was Nìng Zǐ not akin?
Who'd die for Yáng Gē's song?
Restless, not my kind,
Anxious, not of my tribe.
Alas, the matters of glory and shame,
Coming and going, I savor the true Way.
The true Way is truly delightful,
Purity preserves the spirit.
Cháo Yú upheld high virtue,
Henceforth, he went to the river's edge.
Number Seventy-Five
East of the bridge, fragrant grass,
Thrice it blooms in a single day.
Its colors fair, beauty radiant,
Splendor that outshines the city.
But is it for the wise man?
Seduction and flattery arise.
Frivolous for a moment,
How to know a name for ages?
By the road, graceful youths,
Fear only the setting sun and moon.
Where see the ancient tree of myth,
Endlessly vast, without form?
Number Seventy-Six
How can one learn the autumn drive?
Dōngyě ends by the roadside.
With deep lines, fish lurk in abysses,
With set snares, birds soar high.
Floating on a light boat,
Drifting with no sight to behold.
Who benefits from empty praise?
Rivers and lakes forget each other.
Allure is hard to maintain,
Cultivating demeanor is my constant.
This year, amid pines and oaks,
In a daze, truly endless.
Number Seventy-Seven
Alas, I've walked till old,
Striving, often beset by woes.
By the river, I envy great waves,
Same start, different branches flow.
A hundred years, what's to say?
But bitter grievances and feuds.
Who are these foes and resentful ones?
Eyes and ears bring mutual shame.
Sights and sounds drift far apart,
Human feelings press urgently.
Summon those profound seers,
Come and go, rejoicing in wanderings.
Number Seventy-Eight
Once there was an immortal sage,
Who dwelt in Shè Mountain's vale.
Riding clouds, steering flying dragons,
Breathing in, feasting on jade blossoms.
Audible but unseen,
Passionate sighs and laments.
Grieving not to be his equal,
Sorrow and hardship come upon me.
Learning below, understanding above,
In haste, what shall I do?
Number Seventy-Nine
In the woods, a wondrous bird,
Declares itself the phoenix.
At dawn, it drinks from sweet springs,
At dusk, it perches on hilltops.
Its cry echoes through the nine realms,
Craning its neck, gazing over eight wilds.
But when the autumn wind arises,
Its wings are hidden away.
Gone west to Kūnlún,
When will it return to soar?
Only regret its misplaced station,
Sorrow that wounds the heart.
Number Eighty
I step out, gazing for the fair one,
But where is the fair one now?
Three mountains summon Sōng and Qiáo,
For all ages, who to await?
Life and death have their lengths,
In passion, how can I know?
Swiftly the morning sun declines,
Walking on, to where shall I go?
See not the late autumn grass,
Broken now, at this very hour.
Number Eighty-One
Once there were immortals,
Xiànmén along with Sōng and Qiáo.
Breathing in the nine yang realms,
Ascending high, tasting the clouds.
Life's joy lies in longevity,
A hundred years deemed vast.
But the white sun sets in the valley,
One dusk, no dawn returns.
Better to leave worldly things,
Rise bright and drift away.
Number Eighty-Two
Before the tomb, glowing bright,
Hibiscus shines with crimson blooms.
Their glory not lasting a morning,
Gales strip their petals away.
How unlike the western hill's grass,
Lánggān and vermilion grain.
Their shadows fall on Zēngchéng,
Their light illumines the nine slopes.
Better than the fleeting youth,
Whose days pass, hard to lament.
Two Songs
"The Woodcutter's Song"
The sun sets west of Bùzhōu,
The moon emerges from Dānyuān.
Yang essence obscured from sight,
Yin light reigns in its place.
Majestic yet fleeting,
Fading then rising again.
Parting and joining like clouds and mist,
Coming and going like swirling winds.
Wealth and honor in a blink,
Poverty and lowliness need not endure.
Liú Hóu rose from a fugitive,
His might shook the wild frontiers.
Shào Píng, enfeoffed at Dōnglíng,
In one day became a commoner.
Branches and leaves rely on roots,
Life and death share prosperity and decline.
Success follows destiny's ascent,
Failure drifts with time's decay.
Cold and heat march in succession,
Transformations push each other onward.
Fortune and misfortune have no fixed master,
Why worry about having no home?
Ponder this principle,
What sorrow in bearing firewood?
"Song of the Great Man"
Heaven and earth unravel, the cosmos opens,
Stars fall, sun and moon crumble,
Soaring upward, what shall I cherish?
"Rhapsody on Dōngpíng"
The nine provinces have their boundaries,
The nine fields their configurations,
Regions high and low,
All things have their order:
Open them, and they flow;
Block them, and they stagnate;
Channel them, and they move;
Dam them, and they stop;
Raise them, and hills form;
Depress them, and marshes appear;
Winding and spreading,
Encircled by great chasms.
When divided into towns and fiefs,
Marked by boundary posts,
The four seasons display their signs,
Yīn and Yáng circulate their energies,
Interconnecting and swirling,
With form and virtue,
Clouds rise, thunder stirs,
Now loud, now silent;
Some find peace thereby,
Others are led astray.
Observe the gaps in remote corners,
The paths of desolate wilderness,
Realms of vast emptiness,
Cities in barren lands;
Strange and deceptive wonders,
Beyond all depiction.
Then there are wandering scholars,
Cultivated and noble,
Riding fierce gales,
Treading floating skies,
Pure and turbid both fading,
Fortune and misfortune intertwined.
Thus Líng Lún roamed with phoenixes south of Kūnlún,
Zōu Zǐ breathed warmth north of Shǔ Valley,
Bó Gāo ascended Shàngjì's peaks,
Xiànmén wandered freely on triple mountains' ridges;
Soaring to Xuánpǔ above,
Roaming Dènglín below.
Phoenixes sing spontaneously,
Dancing larks soar freely,
Fine grains flourish abundantly,
Yet not our millet or corn.
Its narrow confines hold broad thoroughfares,
Ruins of deer and swine,
No place for purity and elegance,
But where filth accumulates.
Westward, Shǒuyǎng Ā Zhēn,
Connected to Qī Pú nearby,
Among mulberries and Pú's banks,
Dwellings of wanton excess.
Three Jìn states vie for power,
Zhèng and Wèi spread disorder,
Heroes oppress in succession,
Followers linger and reside.
Thus tyranny crosses every threshold,
Resentment flares in bedroom corners,
Villainy born from village feasts,
Needing no time to erupt.
Its soil lies central,
Where Liú and Wáng clans gather.
High cliffs overlook the city,
Boundless streams gird the dwellings.
Shū's marital kin,
Dwell by its shores indeed,
Backed by peril, facing water,
Filthy and full of selfishness.
Thus in its villages and hamlets,
None speak against it,
Twisting feelings and reason,
To amass their wealth.
Its fields lie barren and wild,
Planting misses the seasons,
Farmlands left untilled,
Thorns and brambles unchecked,
Stagnant ponds and leftover pools,
Overflowing without restraint.
East borders Sān Qí,
West connects Zōu and Lǔ,
Long roads stretch a thousand miles,
Hosting merchants and travelers;
Idle strength as the norm,
Officials assist as envoys,
Proud servants in small towns,
Here they make their home.
Rivers and marshes offer shortcuts,
Dòngtíng and Jīng Chǔ,
Lingering customs pass through,
Becoming paths and dwellings.
Following decaying traditions,
No model to observe,
Not adopting righteousness,
Leading thus to cruelty.
Hence they echo and flaunt power,
Turning from reason to wickedness,
Chasing arrogance and profit,
Fearing only punishment.
Their dwellings dark and blocked,
Deep and hidden, unillumined,
Leaning on burial mounds,
Wrapped in winding rooms;
So living there clouds the mind,
Speaking of it saddens the heart,
Fearful and unsettled,
With no awakening or solace.
Beyond, the turbid Huáng River winds its marshes,
The clear Jǐ River washes its banks.
To the north, linked ridges,
Steep and jagged,
Mountains lofty and towering,
Clouds and lightning intermingle,
Strong winds whip fiercely,
Desolate on the great plains.
To the south, the floating Wèn River lies deep,
Flowing puddles form ponds,
Dense woods and lush trees,
Profuse and uneven,
Flocks of birds soar skyward,
All beasts crisscross in haste.
Though the common folk are unvirtuous,
The mountains and marshes suffice to compensate.
Ancient sages valued subtlety,
Cherishing orderly governance and teachings.
What the mysterious truth holds dear,
Is the joy of silence and simplicity.
Lamenting the scattered feelings in alleys,
I raise my voice with the swirling wind.
Gazing on the wild thickets' decay,
I turn to Dōngshān's verdant green.
Savoring the old words of villages,
I compose new poems to console my heart.
Truly, harsh frost has not yet nourished,
How can the crimson tree bloom again?
"The North Gate" grieves with deep worry,
"The Little Pan" mourns in solitary sincerity.
The osprey alone admires benevolence,
Why can't simplicity prevail?
Those feathers inspire reflection,
How much more should people be wise?
In troubled times, I ponder afar,
Longing to return with the gusting wind.
Reverently, I wander hilltops,
Watching these flocks compete in flight.
Things transform, and the spirit rejoices,
Can distant views be pursued?
Riding a pine boat through perilous waters,
Though untethered, I find myself bound.
Galloping a Huáliú steed on a narrow path,
I glance back, unable to outpace a lame donkey.
Adorned with fine caps to visit Yuè,
I see rhinoceros light and enter first;
Clad in embroidered robes to trade with Róng,
I recognize felt garments are sure to be worn.
Upholding the purity of virtuous harmony,
Which land could I call home?
I shall return to noble customs,
And invite the prince to roam with me.
Rinsing my mouth with jade nectar’s soothing taste,
Drinking from clear streams of pure water.
Thus, with humility, I shall persist,
Why cling to worries and fears?
Again I say:
Praising the beauty of the seasons,
Lovely spring warmth heralds summer’s start.
Entrusting my thoughts to the wind, I journey on,
Using my form to complete the ride.
Following leisurely reins, I drive far,
Asking the lost in lush winds.
Dark clouds rise and surround me,
Cold rain falls and descends.
Suddenly awakening, I lose my way,
Treading emptiness, I venture forth.
The whirlwind obscures Héxū,
Xiánchí shines upon Zēngchéng.
Delighting in the morning’s radiant glow,
Rejoicing in the sun’s fiery essence.
Measuring the empty boat with pondering thoughts,
I wander freely in the clear depths.
Heeding the profound truths’ sincere teachings,
I envision the perfected ones in form.
Rarely seeing their intricate details,
My thoughts stretch far, yet measures feel close,
Turning the carriage in field ditches,
As if Kōngsāng were within reach.
Words overflow without cease,
My heart lingers, unending.
Gathering gentle admonitions for reflection,
I lament the unpredictability of public counsel.
My spirit wanders far, yearning to return,
Fearing twin rings at my side.
Sighing at birds that do not flock,
Grieving the endless expanse.
All find wild greens easy to cultivate,
Gathering praise from left and right.
Fearing to drift away with the wind forever,
I entrust myself to Zhuānxū at Fùyú.
Though lutes and zithers all remain,
Could their melodies ever resound again?
Considering travels to seek wonders,
Where would those soaring upward go?
Confusion shrouds in chaotic disorder,
Vast and turbulent, unsettled.
Principles tangled, I change my stance,
Straightening my robes to compose myself.
Setting rules to measure balance,
Consulting my turtle shell for insight.
Gazing where this carriage turns aside,
It’s truly near, not far at all.
How could three years pass without word?
I’ll go once and return nine times.
Looking at the bright sun’s first rays,
Riding winding hills, I adorn my appearance.
As time withers and drifts away,
I test what must follow, flourishing or fading.
Releasing distant, broad measures,
I practice the constant bond of simple vows.
Roaming Xiāngchéng’s leisurely harvest,
Reciting the pure oath left behind.
Drenched by wind and rain,
How dare I soar high to roam officialdom?
Quietly cherishing steadfast devotion,
Peaceful and serene through eternity.
Why linger here to feel sorrow?
I’ll change my visage in foreign lands.
So I choose heights to dwell upon,
Ever joyful, healthy, and content.
"Shǒuyáng Mountain Rhapsody"
In autumn of the first year of Zhèngyuán,
I was still a court gentleman,
In the Grand General’s residence,
Alone, I went south of the wall,
Facing north toward Shǒuyáng Mountain,
And composed this rhapsody:
In the final years of this era,
The month’s start is deeply overcast.
The wind swirls in twisting gusts,
Rain spirals, dampening my robe.
Crickets chirp in the east chamber,
Cuckoos call in the western woods.
As dusk falls with no companion,
Sorrowful thoughts stir my heart.
Shaking my sandy cloak, I step out the door,
My tassels severed, nowhere to be found.
Pacing aimlessly, lost in distant thoughts,
Sighing deeply, I softly chant.
Wishing to refine myself and venture forth,
The crowd jeers and mocks me.
In silent solitude I stand alone,
Clearly rooted in isolation, without cause.
Holding fast to singular devotion,
I despise the false crowd’s attacks on truth.
Faithful and steadfast, never to part,
I’d rather rise high and seclude myself.
Lifting my head to gaze afar,
I behold Shǒuyáng’s ridges and peaks.
Trees cluster lush and leaning,
Rustling crisply, their sounds carried aloft.
Below, rugged with no foothold,
Above, transparent with nothing to cling to.
Phoenixes soar past but do not rest,
Hooting owls flock and roost together.
Drifting far away into the distance,
The two elders, destitute, came home.
Truly confined and dwelling here,
How could they find leisure to dare complain?
Fine grains were hidden, no longer present,
Thus they chose death, gathering ferns.
Those who turned from Yīn to follow Chāng,
Rushed to peril and ruin without delay;
These advanced but found no accord,
How can they be called benevolent and righteous?
Reckless with life and death, unheeding,
They compete in slander and praise as their standard.
Examining past records’ claims,
What noble discourse is worth admiring?
If the Way is sought in minutiae,
Why elaborate with empty words?
Moreover, with clarity and emptiness, I guard my spirit,
How could I speak with fervent passion?
"Dove Rhapsody"
In the Jiāpíng era, I obtained two dove chicks,
Often fed them millet and grains,
Later, they were killed by a dog,
So I composed this rhapsody.
In the blessed years of lush grace,
Vast beginnings emerged faintly, enlightening the obscure.
There were destined, rare birds,
Sharing kinship with the calling dove.
Perching on carved trees in hidden corners,
Nesting high on distant pines;
Breathing mist and clouds for sustenance,
Roaming the morning sun together,
After ten days, they nurtured their kind,
Praising the seven chicks’ graceful forms.
First folding wings and grooming feathers,
They met the bleak autumn wind’s chill.
Already overturned beyond rescue,
Shaken loose, with no aid to uphold them.
Ascending Huán Mountain, lingering there,
Facing their old home, longing to enter;
Raising mournful cries to see them off,
Grieving their departure, never to gather again.
Ultimately drifting and scattered,
Mourning the weak chicks’ trembling sorrow.
On what could they rely for nurture?
Leaning on siblings’ kinship bonds.
Turning from wild grasses to seek virtue;
Sheltering in the noble’s tranquil room,
Savoring the fragrant millet offerings,
Secure by the window, free from harm.
Cleaning feathered robes, necks entwined,
Eschewing lavish brilliance and excess,
Adorning with poised beauty as reflection,
Fond of dignified bearing, ever consistent,
Bowing and rising, carefree and at ease,
Seeking affection and charm in the present day,
Why envy those who soar aloft?
Wishing to repay kindness, forgetting all else.
Encountering a mad dog’s fierce rage,
Violence inflicted on their tiny frames,
Seeking to destroy and obliterate,
They were cast aside and lost forever,
Alas, lamenting their humble frailty,
How could they be forgotten even for a moment?
"Macaque Rhapsody"
In ancient times, Yǔ tamed floods and lands, sending Yì to drive beasts,
Cleansing rivers and valleys, combing forests and hills,
Thus divine marvels took form on the Nine Tripods, and strange creatures arrived.
So the lush fox and patterned leopard shed their coats,
The rare tailed Zōuyú offered its treasures,
Kuāfù and Dúlù cast off their splendor,
Green horses and tri-colored steeds abandoned their herds:
This is how their might led to their demise.
As for the bear and panther roaming by the river,
They display their prowess by braving perils;
The mythical Kuí dwells in the abyss to follow his will,
While Yáng Zhèn's reputation shines though clad in fur.
In open wilderness, some become illustrious,
Why should those in seclusion not follow suit?
The mole fears oppression and hides away,
Burrowing deep into sacred mounds.
Eventually lured by bait for food,
How can mere cave-digging forbid it?
If there truly is profit and desire,
Even rare sightings lead to capture.
Thus, the near ones are not counted in years,
The distant ones do not span ages,
The great are praised for millennia,
The petty are mocked in the present.
The macaque is but a minor example,
Yet it is tethered among the lower ranks.
Its form resembles but is not of the kind,
Its shape divergent and impure.
Outwardly clever but inwardly unmeasured,
Thus human-faced yet beast-hearted.
Narrow-minded and eager for advancement,
Like Hán Fēi imprisoned in Qín,
Raising brows and darting glances,
As if skilled speech masks falseness.
Surrounded by a bustling crowd from behind,
Like felling a tree and losing neighbors.
Adjusting attire in grand robes,
Harboring thoughts of return like Xiàng Yǔ.
Indulging desires with sidelong glances,
Possessing the fair grace of Zhǎng Qīng.
Lifting head and lips in posturing,
Actions may improve and self-renew.
Bathing in orchid-scented water yet growing foul,
Unlike Sòng Cháo's flatterers.
Ends up mocked and in bonds,
Though familiar, never close.
What use are many talents?
Inevitably sullied and demeaned.
Agile and skilled in tricks,
Leaping swiftly over cliffs and crags.
Having fled to the woods eastward,
Then found on the ridge and captured.
Bound by ropes and restrained,
Gazing at the western mountains with long sighs;
Climbing rafters to linger,
How could it forget the Dèng Forest?
Hoping for the noble's favor,
Devising unusual sights to devote heart,
Biding time to pass the long day,
How can joy and pride be indulged?
Thus it dies beneath the hall,
Forever vanishing in form and spirit.

"Qīng Sī Fù"
I believe that what is visible in form,
Is not the beauty of color;
What is audible in sound,
Is not the goodness of music.
In the past, the Yellow Emperor ascended to immortality on Jīng Shān,
Echoing Xiánchí at the ridges of Nán Yuè,
Ghosts and spirits in their obscurity,
Yet Kuí and Yá heard not his melody.
Nǚ Wá shone gloriously by the eastern seas,
And fluttered near the west of the great river,
Forests and stones followed in descent,
But the jade terrace reflected not her light.
Therefore, the subtle has no form,
Silence has no sound,
Only then can one perceive the graceful and pure.
Thus, when the bright sun shines splendidly,
Jì Hòu does not mimic its appearance;
When bells and drums resound harmoniously,
Yán Zǐ does not raise his voice.
For in clear emptiness and vast expanse,
Divine beings gather;
In drifting vagueness and uncertainty,
One penetrates the profound and reaches the dark;
With a heart of ice and jade-like quality,
Purity stirs and thoughts endure;
Serene and without desire,
The will is tranquil and the heart content.
Such inner thoughts are truly fine,
Where then can they not manifest?
The cold wind passes over the millet valley,
Instructing the child to wander with waterfowl.
Shēn Rú grieves as his mother returns,
Wú Hóng mourns as the elephant is born.
This moved feeling reaches the spirits,
How could it be vast and unfulfilled?
Aim not for gain, and the spirit is upright,
Heart not agitated, and it becomes sincere.
Holding fast to unity within,
Able to dwell without faltering.
From clear dawn to evening's calm,
Pointing to Méngsì for eternal peace.
At this time, Xīhé has already declined,
The dark night begins to close,
Wàng Shū prepares the reins,
The plain wind comes on its journey,
Light curtains flutter continuously,
Embroidered mats serene and pure,
Péng Bàng hums softly,
Mole crickets chirp leisurely.
Gazing at Cuīwēi of the southern mountains,
Looking back at the lush green of the northern woods.
The great moon hides behind the rear chambers,
The bright moon shines in the front courtyard.
Then I stretch and lack sleep,
Suddenly awakening with a start.
How can the long spirit then fall silent?
It will converge wherever it goes.
Thoughts wander and change concerns,
The heart trembles and holds reflections.
As if something comes that can be received,
As if something leaves without farewell.
Alas, broad and lowly, losing its course,
Emotions scatter and remain unsoothed.
How can awareness clarify truth?
Truly, it is like the clouds and dreams.
Startled by the strange sounds of creation,
Beholding the exceptional beauty here.
Unfolding the cassia's lute and zither,
Hearing the layered notes of lofty peaks.
Beginning with soft chants and faint echoes,
Feelings quietly wise and subtly stirring.
Then summoning clouds to gather energy,
Shaking and stirring into great awe.
Sounds whistling and vast,
As if ascending Kūnlún and facing the western sea,
Transcending distant obscurity,
Unable to trace its whereabouts.
The heart drifts without anchorage,
Thoughts endless, not half-expressed,
The Dèng Forest perishes in the great marsh,
Qīn Pī mourns by the jade bank.
Wandering hesitantly,
Gracefully spreading wide.
Roaming the plain garden with long gazes,
Riding the adorned banners of lengthy waters.
Longing solemnly for eternal arrival,
Cleansing the great peace of level roads.
Following paths open and directly accessible,
Opening inner doors to deep chambers.
Admiring the ethereal floating,
Leaning on the east wind to radiate light.
Bathing in Wěi Yuān for refined secrecy,
Body pure and beyond reproach.
Adorned with white jade for a face,
Cloaked in crimson clouds for attire.
Donning the radiant essence of nine luminaries,
Wearing Yáoguāng to emit subtlety.
Robed in shimmering splendor,
Gathering myriad hues in harmony.
Colors glistening and resplendent,
Intricately interwoven and lush.
Like morning clouds converging,
Seeming to change in mutual reliance;
Directing Cháng Yí to lead with grace,
Commanding the river maiden to join in return.
Strolling leisurely and advancing uniquely,
Glancing at both pillars ascending steps;
Shaking the jade stream to ring gems,
Sowing Língyáng's elegance.
Treading the perilous traces of melting ice,
Stepping on the lightness of dispersal.
Shedding the vermilion shoes of peaceful courts,
Treading on mats and gathering curtains.
Laying out what comes in the chamber,
Then glimpsed by the fleeting.
Fragrance emanating outward,
Charming face glowing to reveal beauty.
Clear words subtle as orchids,
Speech gentle and unopposing.
Entrusting to the spirits' convergence,
Floating on the lingering glow of sun and moon.
Borrowing the essence of pure energy,
Fortunate to cherish privately,
Wishing to express love tonight,
Yet still inquiring of right and wrong.
Cloaked in evening's fragrant warmth,
About to depart briefly and return forever.
Observing joy not yet stilled,
Words unfinished, heart sorrowful.
Alas, that rainbows could be relied upon,
Yet turning wings to fly away together.
I abandon the cramped central hall,
Leaving behind the dwellings unfit to inhabit.
Curtains are spread but not guarded,
Mats and tables set but unattended.
I mount the misty chariot veiled in clouds,
Riding the two dragons of Xiàhòu,
Breaking off a branch of the Dān tree to shield from the sun,
Raising a triple-layered canopy of lingzhi,
Fluttering and soaring left and right,
Billowing and flowing with graceful ease.
Gazing at the morning clouds in succession,
They resemble a beauty laden with sorrow.
Their colors blend into patterns,
Yet suddenly scatter and vanish without a trace.
As if words were left unspoken,
The mood shifts and drifts away.
Like drooping hair losing its adornment,
Ornaments not yet gathered, the form fades;
Eyes glance and distinguish on their own,
The heart yearns to come, yet the appearance remains distant.
Intricate and exquisite, not fully expressed,
First aligned with the constellations' order.
Times grow dim and overcast,
Suddenly, I no longer recognize the old abode.
I stride to the lofty terrace of the yellow demon,
The thunder god stirs and brings down rain.
Within, the wise and long-lived,
Reprimand the unruly and deceitful.
Crushing demons and breaking spirits,
I ascend directly to where I aspire.
Traversing the four directions with unbridled heart,
Who says I look back with doubt?
Leaping high and racing swiftly,
I reach the North Pole and release all cares.
Grasping the cords of the cosmos to show the way,
I bid farewell at the gate of cold.
Since my heart is not burdened by the myriad things,
How could a single woman be worth longing for!
Kàngfù Rhapsody
"Kàngfù Rhapsody"
I once traveled to Kàngfù,
Ascended its walls,
And it filled me with melancholy thoughts,
So I composed this rhapsody to criticize it,
Declaring it a place of no joy.
Kàngfù is
The destitute land of the Nine Provinces,
A desolate void from ancient times.
Thus, its walls are low, small, and cramped,
Perilously narrow and confined;
Its fields are muddy, clogged with silt,
Mired in filth and muck.
Ponds border it, holding torrents of water,
Foul weeds thrive, inedible and abundant,
The earth lies sunken and shadowy, receiving no harmonious energy,
The sun does not fully shine, so nothing good grows.
Hence, its people are stubborn, foolish, and brutish,
The lowest of the simple, hard to civilize.
Its terrain is blocked and cut off,
Divided and pressed by swirling depths,
End and beginning linked as one,
Root and tip intertwined,
From past to present,
Through empty ages and passing years.
Jùyě Marsh lies behind it,
Exhausted Qí ends before it,
Canals do not flow freely,
Filth and turbidity truly gather,
The unworthy cluster together,
Houses empty, without a single worthy.
Thus, its people wander scattered and disordered,
Dwelling in marshes and hiding in thickets,
Treading the paths of deer,
Sharing the ambitions of fierce beasts.
Therefore, its plains remain uncultivated,
Planting sparse and rare,
Weeds and reeds overrun the hills,
Mosquitoes and gadflies torment the skin.
In its distant perils,
To the right lies Jīnxiāng and to the left Gāopíng,
With towering ridges and majestic peaks,
Deep gorges and precipitous cliffs;
No beauty dwells there,
But bears and tigers are born,
So the people suffer bites and gnawing harm,
Their nature that of birds and beasts.
In its nearby barriers,
Doves shade the front,
Winding walls rise behind;
Owls flock in mournful flight,
Could they have aspirations even for a moment?
Thus, its people have the temper of wolves and the aura of jackals,
Devoid of substance, like fleeting lightning.
To the south, one glimpses Chūnshēn,
To the east, gazes toward Mèngcháng,
Bordered by Xuē County,
Edging Shānyáng;
Inns for travelers,
Hideouts for thieves and villains.
To the north, it faces Pínglù,
The western frontier of Qí;
A shortcut to Yān and Zhào,
Where fugitives roam free;
Thus, its people are deceitful and crooked,
Concealing and unjust,
Harboring selfishness and fraud,
Following duplicity and concealment,
Rituals and righteousness unestablished,
Unyielding to honest transformation.
Ancient sages left words,
Some clear, some deaf.
How can a noble man
Linger in such a land!
"Memorial Urging the Prince of Jìn on Behalf of Zhèng Chōng"
Chōng and others, guilty of a capital offense.
We humbly observe the illustrious decree has arrived,
And privately hear that Your Excellency firmly declines.
We, Chōng and others, with earnest concern,
Truly hold a simple view:
That when a sage king establishes institutions,
A hundred generations share the same customs,
Praising virtue and rewarding merit,
Has been the practice since ancient times.
In the past, Yī Yǐn,
Was but a humble retainer of the Yǒushēn clan,
Yet once he aided Chéng Tāng,
He was honored with the title "Ā Héng";
Zhōu Gōng, leveraging an established position,
And resting on secured achievements,
Brilliantly resided in Qūfù,
Possessing the lands of Guī and Méng;
Lǚ Shàng,
A fisherman of Pánxī,
With one wave of his command,
Was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū.
Since then,
Those with meager merits yet rich rewards are countless,
Yet wise and philosophical men still regard it as a noble tale.
How much more, since the time of the late Prime State,
Has there been a lineage of illustrious virtue,
Assisting the Wèi house,
To pacify the world,
With no flawed governance in court,
No slander among the people.
Previously, Your Excellency campaigned west to Língzhōu,
North to the deserts,
West of Yúzhōng,
All trembled in submission at the mere news,
The Qiāng tribes raced eastward,
Turning their heads to submit;
In the east, you punished rebels,
Your army alone achieved victory,
Capturing the generals of Hélǘ,
Slaying countless tens of thousands of swift and sharp troops,
Your might extended to the Southern Sea,
Your name awed the Three Yuè;
The realm enjoyed peace and prosperity,
No tyranny or evil arose,
Thus, distant customs feared your authority,
The eastern barbarians offered their dances.
Therefore, the Sacred Emperor, reviewing past rituals and ancient statutes,
Establishes a state and glorious seat,
Manifesting this Tàiyuán.
Your Excellency should heed the sacred decree,
Accept this great blessing,
Truly fitting for both heaven and man.
Such grand achievements and glorious merits;
Such magnificent rewards and exalted fiefs,
Harmony within and without,
Without fault or transgression.
From this, on campaigns,
You could cross the river in court attire,
Sweeping away Wú and Kuài;
Blocking the western source of the river,
Offering sacrifices while gazing at Mín Mountain;
Turning spears and halting chariots to command the world,
The distant none不服,
The near none不respectful,
Making the virtue of great Wèi,
Outshine that of Táng and Yú,
Your Excellency's splendid merits,
Surpass Huán and Wén.
Then, facing the blue isles, you may decline like Zhī Bó,
Ascending Jī Mountain, pay homage to Xǔ Yóu,
How magnificent would that be!
Utmost impartiality and fairness,
Who could compare!
Why trouble with trivial refusals!
Chōng and others fail to grasp the greater principles,

Memorial to Duke Jiǎng Declining an Official Appointment
"Memorial to Duke Jiǎng Declining an Official Appointment"
Your servant Jí prostrates with deepest reverence.
I consider that Your Excellency, possessing unified virtue,
occupies the highest ministerial position,
where all outstanding talents crane their necks in anticipation,
and worthy men of virtue eagerly await.
When your office was established,
every person assumed they would serve as your subordinate;
yet when the appointment letter first descended,
this humble walker was placed at the forefront.
In ancient times, when Zǐxià resided by the Western River, Marquis Wén wielded a broom to welcome him;
when Zōu Yǎn dwelled in the shade of Shǔ Valley, King Zhāo accompanied him in his carriage.
For scholars clothed in plain cloth and leather girdles,
living in solitude and independence,
the reason why kings and dukes humble themselves to approach them
is because the Way resides within them.
Now I, Jí, lack the virtue of Zōu or Bǔ Shāng,
yet possess their simplicity,
and am unworthily troubling you with great courtesy—
how can I bear this?
I plan to till the soil on the sunny side of Eastern Mound,
deliver the surplus tax of millet and grain,
to avoid the path of those in power.
Burdened with firewood, weary and ill,
my foot strength is not robust;
the summons to fill an official post
is something I cannot endure.
I beg to decline this misplaced favor,
to glorify your pure recommendation.

Letter to Jìn Wén Wáng Recommending Lú Bō
"Letter to Jìn Wén Wáng Recommending Lú Bō"
I have heard that promoting transformation and aiding governance
lies in obtaining the right people;
gathering the extraordinary and elevating the exceptional
is the lofty aim of sages and worthies.
Thus, when the Eight Scholars returned to Zhōu,
the Way of Zhōu became prosperous;
when Yú Shùn was elevated,
all the Yuán and Kǎi served.
I consider Your Excellency, Duke and Marquis,
endowed with imperial spirit and outstanding beauty,
your nine virtues shine far and wide,
responding to the era as a pillar of support,
discoursing on the Way and spreading transformation,
opening the four gates,
welcoming and admitting winged wise scholars
to assist in harmonious prosperity.
Thus, outstanding and brilliant scholars wish to push open the imperial gates,
inscribe their names and offer their service,
true and straightforward talents converge upon your great office;
indeed, it is like the Dèng Forest, Kūnwú, where the soaring phoenix perches;
the market of xuánlí gems,
where chuíjí treasures gather.
I humbly observe the Assistant Inspector of my humble province,
Lú Bō of the same commandery,
aged thirty-two,
courtesy name Jǐngxuān.
In youth, he possessed extraordinary talent and brilliance,
in adulthood, he harbors the measure of virtue and excellence;
devoted to the Way and delighting in ritual,
he upholds righteousness and relies on benevolence;
he delves deeply into the ancient classics,
ascending the hall and glimpsing the abstruse;
his clear discernment penetrates the principles of things,
his mind comprehends the mysterious and subtle.
His steadfastness is sufficient to manage affairs,
his loyalty and reverence sufficient to solemnize the court,
his clear judgment sufficient to resolve doubts,
his discretion sufficient to respond to changing circumstances,
facing troubles without confusion,
in urgency, his clarity increases.
If given the chance to assist in governing and managing affairs,
he is a vessel for administrative matters;
if entrusted with missions and diplomatic banquets,
he has the talent for independent responses.
Devoting himself to charts and records,
he is a master of literature;
composing elegant writings and records,
he exemplifies a good historian.
Yet his learning is not for self-promotion,
his conduct does not seek advancement,
thus he has long remained submerged,
not yet reaching the highest clarity.
Truly, he is the outstanding and great talent of the later generation,
a sharp tool of the current time,
deserving of commendation and appointment,
to harmonize the flavors at the tripod and lever.
Confucius said:
"If I praise someone,
it must be after testing them."
Lú Bō's abilities
are evident in his past achievements.
I dare not embellish falsely,
to invite criticism upon your great office.

"Reply to Fú Yì's Letter"
Jí states:
Having received your message and understood your intent,
my heart is moved to trace its path.
The height of the nine heavens—
swift-feathered birds cannot find its peak;
the depth of the four seas—
deep-dwelling fish cannot fathom its bottom;
how much less can one of no feathery distinction discuss it!
Moreover, dark clouds have no fixed form,
the responding dragon has no constant appearance:
at times they dawn and vanish by dusk,
suddenly alternating in rise;
at times they wallow in mud or soar skyward,
descending at dawn, rising by night,
stretching their bodies, the eight dimensions cannot contain their traces,
contracting their joints, the smallest间隙 allows ease;
this, again, the blind cannot behold,
the petty insects cannot comprehend.
Thus, those who cultivate profundity and vastness
cannot be fathomed by shallow strength;
those of spiritual transformation and divine change
cannot be discerned by limited vessels.
Why must you, sir, so earnestly seek my true essence!
Human capabilities and circumstances cannot be equal,
preferences and inclinations differ.
The luán and fèng phoenixes dance on wings above the celestial river,
while turtledoves and sparrows delight in soaring over overgrown woods;
the hornless dragon floats in eight marshes to wash its scales,
while turtles enjoy frolicking in puddles and departing in groups;
each follows their own affections to seek joy.
To affirm this and deny that—
how can they be made equal?
When a person establishes their integrity,
they aim to spread a net to encompass the world,
how could they cautiously entangle themselves in its meshes?
Just as opening a mold to shape customs,
what need is there to destroy one's essence to conform to scrutiny?
If favorable fortune does not align,
and divine mechanisms lack clarity,
then soar with spirit and uphold ambition,
transcending the world with lofty detachment,
floating essence rises beyond the realm of mystery,
unfolding wondrous integrity beyond the nine heavens, riding the light, leaping and prancing,
bounding over the vague and vast,
composedly wandering with the transformations of the Dao,
freely roaming alongside the sun and moon,
mingling with the formless to share in change,
and joining the illustrious spirits to equalize transformations,
ascending to where there is no higher,
descending to where there is no lower,
dwelling where there is no abode,
emerging where there is no gate,
harmonizing with the coming and going of all things,
following the emptiness and fullness of the six energies,
gathering the dark net at the Great Ultimate,
caressing the unity of heaven in the vast expanse,
floating dust cannot stir its waves,
flying grime cannot soil its purity,
merely lodging the physical form in this realm,
how can the spirit be fully perceived?
Although no deed goes unheard,
and no strategy unacknowledged,
yet understanding has its limits,
which is not to be wondered at.
Observing the pursuits of the gentleman:
wishing to flaunt gold that topples cities,
yet seeking a sale for a hundred coins;
fabricating rites that reach the heavens,
but imitating checks of an inch's breadth;
laboring the royal person to serve things,
clinging to foulness to exhaust oneself;
sinking in the shallow footprints of oxen,
fretting over the rootlessness of the Milky Way;
their baseness is shameful,
their endeavors pitiable.

affirms the vast profundity of the great Dao,
so confine your steps to the common path,
and do not trouble yourself with distant thoughts.

my strength to explain is limited.
